- There was no revenue-growth driver shared by all four companies in FY2024–FY2025: Intel’s revenue declined in both years. FY2024 revenue was $53.1 billion versus $54.2 billion in FY2023; FY2025 revenue fell another $248 million to $52.9 billion. [S19] [S72]

- The strongest common drivers applied to subsets:
  - AI and data-center demand — NVIDIA and AMD. NVIDIA’s FY2024 growth reflected demand for AI infrastructure; FY2025 growth was driven by accelerated computing, Hopper platforms and AI networking. AMD’s FY2024–FY2025 Data Center growth reflected higher sales and demand for Instinct GPUs and EPYC processors. This was not a demonstrated all-company driver. [S35] [S37] [S41] [S68]
  - Higher shipment volumes and stronger product demand — across different businesses. NVIDIA’s FY2024 Gaming growth benefited from normalized channel inventory and growing demand. AMD’s Client growth in both years reflected higher Ryzen shipments and selling prices. Intel’s FY2024 notebook growth benefited from improved customer inventory levels, despite declining consolidated revenue. Qualcomm’s FY2025 growth benefited from premium Android demand, higher IoT shipments and automotive launches. [S35] [S41] [S70] [S20] [S61]
  - Higher-value product mix and pricing — AMD, Intel and Qualcomm. AMD reported higher Client selling prices in FY2024 and FY2025; Intel’s FY2024 server revenue benefited from a higher mix of high-core-count products; Qualcomm’s FY2025 handset growth benefited from higher prices and favorable mix. [S41] [S70] [S20] [S61]
  - Automotive expansion — NVIDIA and Qualcomm. NVIDIA’s FY2024 automotive growth reflected self-driving platforms; Qualcomm’s FY2025 automotive growth reflected shipments for new Snapdragon digital-cockpit vehicle launches. [S35] [S61]

- Bottom line: stronger demand and product adoption were recurring themes, but the evidence does not support one universal cause—or revenue growth at every company. [S35] [S41] [S61] [S72]
